youtube.title: Oldest Shipwreck Ever Found: Why Is There No Ship?
youtube.description:
The oldest shipwreck ever found was just announced off Turkey, and there is no ship in it. So how do archaeologists know how old it is?

Near Kekova Island, about 30 meters down, divers from Akdeniz University found more than 30 clay storage jars and three stone anchors. The wooden hull rotted away long ago, so the team dated the wreck by the shape of its Early Bronze Age jars: roughly 4,500 years old, from the age of the pyramids. If that date holds, this ancient shipwreck beats the old record from Dokos in Greece by centuries.

Subscribe to Stickstory for a strange true story every day. What do you think was inside those jars: wine, olive oil or something else? Tell me in the comments!

scenes.text: The world's oldest shipwreck has no ship.
scenes.visual: Underwater, 30 m down: clay jars and stone anchors lie scattered on the sand; above them a dashed ghost outline of a ship draws itself in where the hull should be, and on 'no' a big red X slashes across it; the fez narrator in front swims with bubbles and jumps back in shock.

scenes.text: Divers found it off Turkey, thirty meters down.
scenes.visual: Old map of Turkey's coast: a red dot pops at Kekova on the southern shore with a hand-written note '30 m down'; the fez narrator below points at it.

scenes.text: And what was left? More than thirty clay jars and three stone anchors.
scenes.visual: On the sea floor the belted clay jars pop up one after another while a big counter runs to '30+ JARS'; then three slab stone anchors with rope holes pop in front; the fez narrator swims down from above and points at them.

scenes.text: But the wooden hull? Gone, rotted away long ago.
scenes.visual: A wooden hull full of jars lies on the sand; on 'Gone' a red stamp 'GONE' slams in and the planks crumble one by one into drifting flecks, the ribs fade, the jars drop onto the sand; only a dashed outline is left; the fez narrator shrugs.

scenes.text: So how do you date a ship that isn't there?
scenes.visual: On a quiet, empty beach the fez narrator walks in and on 'date' holds up a sign 'AGE = ?', puzzled; empty sea behind him, no ship anywhere.

scenes.text: Here's the clever part: you read the jars.
scenes.visual: Close-up of one big belted clay jar on the sand; a red ring circles its raised clay belt and a hand-written red note 'clay belt' with an arrow points at it; the fez narrator peers at it through his spyglass, then points.

scenes.text: This shape of jar dates to about 4,500 years ago,
scenes.visual: Vertical timeline: 'c. 2500 BC jar made' in red, then 'c. 2200 BC Greek wreck' (the old record), then '2026 announced'; the fez narrator beside it points back at 2500 BC.

scenes.text: when Egypt was building the pyramids.
scenes.visual: Desert horizon at Giza: three pyramids rise, the biggest still unfinished with a mud-brick ramp and tiny workers hauling a block up it; a belted jar pops up in the foreground; the fez narrator points up at the pyramids and a note 'SAME ERA' appears.

scenes.text: If that holds, it beats the old record from Greece by centuries.
scenes.visual: Board 'Oldest wrecks': bar 'Turkey' ~4,500 years grows longer than bar 'Greece' ~4,200 years, then a red pill 'NEW RECORD' pops; the fez narrator at the bottom right points at it.

scenes.text: The wood forgot this ship. The clay never did.
scenes.visual: Giant words build up: 'THE CLAY / NEVER FORGOT' with 'CLAY' in a red box; the big fez narrator below points at it, smiling.
